content: For young children aged 12–23 months who are not breastfed, animal milk is recommended as a source of nutrition. Follow-up formulas are not advised due to low certainty of evidence supporting their benefits. Dairy products, including liquid animal milk, are an essential part of a diverse diet and contribute to nutritional adequacy. This is particularly important for non-breastfed children when other animal-source foods (ASFs) are unavailable. Acceptable types of animal milk include pasteurized animal milk, reconstituted evaporated milk (not condensed milk), fermented milk, or yogurt. Flavored or sweetened milks should be avoided. For infants aged 6–11 months who are fed animal milk, full-fat milk should be used. Safe storage and handling practices for animal milk must be followed. The Guideline Development Group (GDG) found insufficient evidence to recommend full-fat versus low-fat milk or animal milk versus plant-based milk for children aged 12–23 months. Sweetened milks, which contain added sugars, are not appropriate for infants and young children aged 6–23 months. Not all infants and young children are breastfed between 6 and 23 months due to various reasons, such as lack of a supportive environment, maternal choice, or medical conditions. Some breastfed children also receive other milks. Milk or another source of dairy is necessary for all children aged 6–23 months. For breastfed children, this is primarily breast milk, though other dairy foods can be part of a diverse diet. For non-breastfed children, milk or another source of dairy is essential, especially if they are not consuming other animal-source foods. According to the 2016 Lancet Breastfeeding Series, 37% of children aged 6–23 months in lowand middle-income countries (LMICs) do not receive breast milk, with rates varying from 18% in low-income countries to 55% in high-income countries. In such cases, milk formula, animal milk, or another dairy source is needed to meet the unique nutritional needs of this age group. Animal milk is a significant source of key nutrients, including protein, calcium, riboflavin, potassium, phosphorus, magnesium, and zinc. Milk protein stimulates insulin-like growth factor-1, which is important for bone mass acquisition and growth. Most milk formulas are derived from cow’s milk, though some are plant-based. These formulas are designed to be as nutritionally similar to breast milk as possible but lack its immunological properties and some nutrients. Milk formulas have been aggressively marketed and are associated with child morbidity and mortality, leading to the establishment of the International Code of Marketing of Breast-milk Substitutes by the World Health Assembly in 1981. The use of cow’s milk in infancy has been linked to gastrointestinal blood loss and iron deficiency anemia (IDA), though the duration of this association is unclear. It is also associated with increased solute load for the kidneys during this period. Despite these outcomes, opinions differ on the nutritional and health impacts of feeding cow’s milk to infants aged 6–11 months. The WHO Guiding Principles for Feeding Non-breastfed Children 6–24 Months of Age state that feeding animal milk and appropriate complementary foods is a safe choice, as occult blood losses in infants aged 6–11 months are minimal and unlikely to affect iron status. Iron deficiency can be prevented through iron supplements or complementary foods with adequate iron bioavailability. For infants older than 6 months, the WHO Guidelines for HIV and Infant Feeding recommend commercial infant formula or boiled animal milk as acceptable alternatives to breastfeeding, provided specific home conditions are met. These include access to safe water and sanitation, sufficient formula to support normal growth and development, and the ability to prepare it cleanly and frequently to minimize the risk of diarrhea and malnutrition. For young children aged 12–23 months, animal milk is commonly used to support growth and development. There is debate about whether children consuming animal milk should switch to lower-fat milk to reduce saturated fat intake. Some countries recommend whole milk until 24 months of age and low-fat milk thereafter. WHO guidelines suggest reducing saturated fat intake to less than 10% of total energy intake and replacing it with polyunsaturated fats, monounsaturated fats from plant sources, or carbohydrates from foods rich in dietary fiber, such as whole grains, vegetables, fruits, and pulses. Some milks are fortified with additional nutrients and marketed as follow-up formulas, which are widely consumed. However, the composition of these formulas varies significantly, and some contain high levels of protein, carbohydrates, and added sugars. The Codex Alimentarius Commission defines follow-up formula as a food intended for use as part of the weaning diet for infants from 6 months onward and for young children. WHO and many pediatric societies consider these products unnecessary and do not recommend them. In 2016, WHO clarified that toddler milk formulas are breast-milk substitutes and should be regulated under the Code. Plant-based milks, such as soy or almond milk, are increasingly marketed, raising questions about their suitability for young children. Compared to plant-based milk, dairy milk provides more energy, fat, high-quality protein, and essential vitamins and minerals. A systematic review on milks for infants aged 6–11 months found that cow’s milk compared to milk formula may increase the risk of anemia and IDA and result in lower serum ferritin concentrations. Results for hemoglobin concentrations were mixed. No differences were found in anthropometric or developmental outcomes, gastrointestinal blood loss, or diarrhea. The certainty of evidence for all outcomes was graded as very low or low. For children aged 12–23 months, a systematic review identified five studies comparing animal milk to follow-up formula. Children consuming animal milk were more likely to have lower vitamin D concentrations and vitamin D deficiency. Indicators of iron status were also generally poorer among children consuming animal milk compared to follow-up formula. No differences were found in child development indicators. Evidence for all outcomes was rated as low to moderate certainty. The GDG concluded that there is uncertainty in the balance of benefits and harms of animal milk compared to milk formula for infants aged 6–11 months and follow-up formula for children aged 12–23 months, as this balance varies by context. However, there was some agreement that milk formula may offer benefits for infants aged 6–11 months compared to animal milk. For children aged 12–23 months, animal milk is generally a suitable alternative to follow-up formula.
